chunks: Clock and analog on adjacent layers. The question: If I have two traces on adjacent layers, one a clock and another a sensitive analog signal. How should I route these signals?
Suppose two signal layers sit back to back with no ground plane between them.
A clock trace (a fast on-off timing signal) on one layer and an analog trace (a small, smoothly varying signal) on the other then form a tiny capacitor wherever they overlap.
The fixes, best first, are a ground plane between the layers, crossing at 90 degrees so the overlap is tiny, and keeping the traces apart sideways.
Imagine a drummer upstairs and a reader downstairs, separated only by a thin floor. The more floor they share, the more thumping comes through.
If the drummer is over just one corner, little gets through. A thick carpet between them, which is the ground plane, helps most.
Top view of two adjacent layers superimposed.
Parallel routing makes the overlap equal to the full trace length; a perpendicular crossing makes it a single square of trace width squared.
Adjacent layers: two inner signal layers separated only by a thin insulating layer. Dielectric: that insulating layer between conductors.
Capacitance: two conductors that overlap with insulation between them form a capacitor. More overlap area and less spacing mean more capacitance.
90-degree crossing: running one trace straight across the other, so they overlap only in a small square.
Take two traces 0. 2 mm wide, separated by 0. 2 mm of insulation. If they run together for 50 mm, the capacitance is about 1. 9 picofarads (picofarads, trillionths of a farad).
The analog node has 10 picofarads to ground. A 3. 3 volts clock edge divides by the capacitances, so the analog node jumps by about 3. 3 times 1. 86 / 11. 86 = 0. 52 volts .
If the traces instead cross at 90 degrees, the overlap is only 0. 2 mm times 0. 2 mm. That is about 7 fF (femtofarads, thousandths of a pF), and the jump falls to about 2.
4 millivolts , 250 times smaller. That is the whole idea: overlap area sets the coupling, so remove the overlap or put a plane in the way.
"Directly overlapping traces on adjacent layers form a parallel-plate capacitor, so the clock injects C dv/dt into the analog node: roughly 1.
9 picofarads over 50 mm, which can put half a volt on a 10 picofarads node. Best fix is a ground plane between the layers.
If that's not possible, cross them at 90 degrees so the overlap is a tiny square, about 250 times less capacitance, and keep them laterally separated.
Then slow the clock edge, lower the analog node's impedance, and filter at the ADC."
Quick check. Two traces on adjacent layers with no plane between them run parallel for 50 mm. What is the dominant coupling mechanism?
